Where it began

Mohammad Nabi was born in Logar Province, Afghanistan, on 1 January 1985. His family moved to Peshawar in Pakistan when he was young, and it was there, at about ten, that he started to play. When the family came home in 2000 he began playing alongside several who would become the backbone of the national side: Mohammad Shahzad, Asghar Afghan and Shapoor Zadran among them.

Those were lean days. The team had to buy its kit from its neighbours. In 2006, in a tour match against the MCC in Mumbai, Nabi hit 116, and Mike Gatting took note. That led to a place on the MCC's Young Cricketers programme in England, and to his first-class debut in 2007.

The player

Nabi was there for the whole climb. Afghanistan won World Cricket League Division Five in 2008, then Division Four, where he was player of the tournament, then Division Three. In 2009 they played their first One Day International, against Scotland, and Nabi marked the day with a half-century and the match award. He led the side at the 2014 Asia Cup, where they beat Bangladesh, and at the 2015 World Cup.

On 14 June 2018 he played in Afghanistan's first Test, against India. He played 3 Tests in all, to 2019, taking 8 wickets at 31.75 with a best of 3 for 36. He then left the long game to concentrate on the shorter forms.

What made him special

He was a hard-hitting batsman and a canny off-spinner, and his country leaned on both. In 2018 he became the first Afghan bowler to reach 100 one-day international wickets, and that August the first Afghan to play 100 one-day internationals. In 2023 his runs and wickets helped Afghanistan to their first ever win over Pakistan.

The five-day game did not see his best. His 33 Test runs came at 5.50, a tally he could manage in a few overs on a good day in a T20.

Away from the middle

Few cricketers have packed a bag as often. He played franchise cricket in Bangladesh, Pakistan, India, the Caribbean, Australia and England, and in 2017 he became the first Afghan player to be bought at an Indian Premier League auction. In 2016 he won a Pakistan Super League game for Quetta Gladiators by hitting four off the final ball.

And finally

By June 2024 he had been part of Afghan sides that had beaten 45 different nations, from Bahrain and Botswana to Australia and England. That is a lot of opponents for a man whose team once had to buy its bats from across the border.
